name: English Vermilion
lede: English Vermilion is a dulled, brick-leaning red from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, a quieter cousin of true vermilion, the bright red mercury-sulfide pigment.

sections.title: A national variant of vermilion
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary places English Vermilion at plate 3, L 10 [1]. The name marks it as a national variant of [[vermilion]], the pigment long made from mercury sulfide, the same naming pattern as other country-specific vermilions in the period's color trade [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 would call this family a strong red, though this exact entry has no ISCC-NBS block of its own in our library [1].

Its nearest library neighbor is [[dull-red]], and the closest core app color is [[crimson]], about six units away [1]. Maerz and Paul also record a related name, Crimson Lake, first used around 1550, nearly four centuries before this entry's own 1930 date [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this red in 51 of 23,781 paintings, about a fifth of one per cent [2]. The earliest match is a 1324 Coronation of the Virgin, six centuries before the 1930 dictionary date, so that is a lookalike hue and not a record of any named pigment, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. The 1300s and 1400s show the strongest lift, each at more than triple the paintings' overall baseline [2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings; a color match is not proof that vermilion, English or otherwise, was the pigment used [2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[2].
